# Computers
Programmable computers run programs that the crew write themselves. Anyone can walk up to one, read its manual, write a program and run it, whether that's a calculator, a network scanner or a whole new operating system.
## Getting started - Give the computer power. It boots its operating system, [bold]Gridline OS 4.2[/bold], and waits at a prompt. - Click the computer to open its terminal. Type a command and press [bold]Enter[/bold]. Everyone at the same computer sees the same screen. - Type [mono]help[/mono] for the shell's commands, and [mono]man[/mono] for the manual. The manual is on every computer and goes into more detail than these pages. - Every computer comes with a [mono]readme.txt[/mono] and an [mono]examples[/mono] folder: try [mono]cat readme.txt[/mono] and [mono]ls examples[/mono].
## Your first program - [mono]new hello[/mono] writes a starting program, [mono]hello.wire[/mono]. - [mono]build hello.wire[/mono] turns it into a program, [mono]hello.bin[/mono]. - [mono]run hello.bin[/mono] runs it.
Programs are written in [textlink="Wire" link="WireProgramming"], a small language that looks like Python. Edit them on the computer with [mono]nano FILE[/mono].
## The disk Each computer has its own disk of 1 MiB and up to 64 files. Files survive power cuts and go wherever the computer goes. File names can include folders, like [mono]examples/hello.wire[/mono].
## Under the hood Compiled programs, the [mono].bin[/mono] files, are WebAssembly modules. The server runs each one in a sandbox: - every call into a program has a budget of about two million instructions, and a program that runs over is stopped; - a program's memory is capped at 8 MiB; - all computers together share a small slice of each server tick, so no number of busy computers can slow the game down.
A misbehaving program only ever hurts itself: an endless loop is stopped on its first go, and everything else carries on.
